hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? when you’re sad, do you let yourself cry?
options: good. today, someone very strong did too.
a lot of us do. today’s story might loosen that a little.
fair. today, someone cried in front of everyone.

steps.line: In Medina, late in his life, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ had a baby boy. “I named him after my father Ibrahim,” he told his friends: the prophet Abraham.
Little Ibrahim was nursed by a blacksmith’s family out by the palm groves. The Prophet ﷺ would walk out to their smoky house just to pick him up and kiss him.
Ibrahim was not yet two when he fell ill. The Prophet ﷺ came and held him as he was leaving this world, and his eyes filled with tears.

steps.q: A companion is surprised: “Even you, O Messenger of God?” What do you think the Prophet ﷺ calls his tears?
o: Mercy
A weakness he must overcome
A test he is failing
steps.why: “It is mercy,” he answered (Bukhari 1303). The tears came from the same place as his kindness.

steps.line: Then more tears came, and he said: “The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord. O Ibrahim, we are grieved by your separation.”

steps.q: He wept, and in the same breath said he would only say what pleases God. What does that show?
o: Grief and trust can live in one heart
He stopped crying so he could say it
Words matter to God, tears don’t
steps.why: He didn’t choose between them. The tears stayed, the heartache stayed, and so did his trust in God.

steps.line: That same day, the sun went dark over Medina: an eclipse. People began to say the sky was grieving for the Prophet’s ﷺ son.

steps.q: It would have been a comforting story. What do you think the Prophet ﷺ tells them?
o: Yes, even the sky mourns him
It doesn’t happen for anyone’s death or life
Nothing, and lets them believe it
steps.why: “The sun and the moon do not eclipse for the death or the life of anyone,” he said (Bukhari 1043, 1060). When you see it, pray and call on God.

steps.line: He told them: the sun and the moon don’t go dark for anyone’s death or life. They are signs of God. When you see one, pray and call on Him.

steps.q: Why correct them, on one of the hardest days of his life?
o: He wouldn’t let even his grief bend the truth
He wanted people to stop talking about Ibrahim
He was angry at the crowd
steps.why: He could grieve as a father and still be honest as a prophet. His loss didn’t need the sky to make it real.

steps.line: Ibrahim was buried in al-Baqi, beside the Prophet’s ﷺ mosque. And the Prophet ﷺ said his little son had someone to nurse him in Paradise.

steps.pre: When Muslims hear of a death, they say words from the Qur’an: “We belong to God, and to Him we
o: return
pray
submit
steps.why: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji‘un (2:156). The Qur’an gives these words to the patient, and promises them blessings and mercy.

steps.q: In the Qur’an, the prophet Ya‘qub grieves for years for his lost son Yusuf. What happens to his eyes?
o: They turn white from sorrow
He never once cries
He hides them from his family
steps.why: “His eyes became white with grief” (12:84). The same Ya‘qub calls his patience sabrun jamil, beautiful patience (12:83). Tears and patience, together.

steps.line: Today, when someone dies, many Muslims bring food to the family. The Prophet ﷺ asked for it once: “Make food for Ja‘far’s family. What has come to them is enough to keep them busy.”
steps.label: today

steps.q: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: patience that keeps hold of God
mercy, what he called his tears
steps.why: Three words for one day in Medina: the tears were rahma, the holding on was sabr, and inna lillahi is what Muslims still say.

say: here’s what i love. the most important man in medina cried in front of everyone, and didn’t hide it. when someone was surprised, he gave the tears a name: mercy.
in islam, sabr, patience, doesn’t mean a dry face. it means you grieve and still hold on to God. the tears and the trust sat in one heart, on the same day.

steps.q: Another saying teaches that real patience is shown “at the first stroke” of loss. So is crying the opposite of patience?
o: No: tears are mercy; patience is not turning against God
Yes: true patience means no tears at all
Only if you cry where others can see
steps.why: Most scholars teach that tears and a grieving heart are allowed, as he ﷺ wept. What the sayings warn against is wailing, tearing clothes, or words of protest against God.

today.say: it’s okay to cry. and if someone near you is grieving, you don’t need perfect words. sit with them, bring something to eat, say their person’s name. if you pray, a du‘a for them is your choice too.
options: then go gently. showing up is most of it.
i’m so sorry. your tears are mercy too. take all the time you need.

sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1303 (Anas: they went with the Prophet to Abu Sayf the blacksmith, husband of Ibrahim’s wet nurse; he took Ibrahim, kissed and smelled him; later Ibrahim was breathing his last and the Prophet’s eyes shed tears; ‘Abd al-Rahman ibn ‘Awf: “Even you, O Messenger of Allah?”; “O Ibn ‘Awf, it is mercy”; “The eyes shed tears and the heart grieves, and we will not say except what pleases our Lord. O Ibrahim, we are grieved by your separation”)
Sahih Muslim 2315 (“A boy was born to me tonight and I named him after my father Ibrahim”; the same words at his death)

Sahih Muslim 2316 (Anas: no one more compassionate to children; Ibrahim was nursed in the upper part of Medina; the house was full of smoke because the foster father was a blacksmith; he would take him and kiss him)

Sahih al-Bukhari 1043 and 1060 (al-Mughira ibn Shu‘ba: the sun eclipsed on the day Ibrahim died and people said it was because of his death; “The sun and the moon do not eclipse because of the death or life of anyone. When you see them, pray and invoke Allah”)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1382 (al-Bara’: when Ibrahim died, the Prophet said, “There is a wet nurse for him in Paradise”)
Burial in al-Baqi: Ibn Sa‘d, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (Ibrahim buried in al-Baqi); widely reported in the sira
Qur’an 2:155–157 (“Lo! we are Allah’s and lo! unto Him we are returning,” Pickthall; blessings and mercy for the patient)
Qur’an 12:83–86 (Ya‘qub: “comely patience”; “his eyes were whitened with the sorrow”; “I expose my distress and anguish only unto Allah,” Pickthall)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1283 and 1302 (patience is at the first stroke of a calamity)
Sahih al-Bukhari 1294 (not of us is one who slaps the cheeks, tears the clothes, or calls out with the calls of ignorance)
Sunan Abi Dawud 3132; Jami‘ at-Tirmidhi 998 (“Prepare food for the family of Ja‘far, for there has come to them what keeps them occupied”; graded hasan)
check: Ibrahim’s age at death is reported as about sixteen to eighteen months; caption 3 says “not yet two”. Confirm.

Caption 3 says the Prophet ﷺ “held him” as he died. Bukhari 1303 has him take and kiss Ibrahim on an earlier visit, then find him breathing his last; other reports place Ibrahim in his lap. Confirm the wording.
Caption 1’s “my father Ibrahim” follows Muslim 2315 (forefather Abraham); the caption explains it. Confirm.
Caption 2 compresses Muslim 2316 (the blacksmith’s smoky house in the upper part of Medina) to “out by the palm groves”. Confirm.
Burial in al-Baqi is from the sira (Ibn Sa‘d), not the Bukhari reports; caption 7 and the guide’s “why i brought you” line both state it. Confirm.

The eclipse is often identified with the annular eclipse of 27 January 632 (late 10 AH); the lesson gives no date. Bukhari 1043/1060 is al-Mughira’s report; the caption does not say whether he spoke before or after the eclipse prayer. Confirm.
The Ya‘qub question reads “his eyes became white with grief” (12:84); many commentators take it as loss of sight from weeping. Confirm the wording.

The last question’s why gives the mainstream position (tears allowed; wailing, tearing clothes and protest against God warned against, Bukhari 1294). Confirm it reads gently for someone grieving right now.
